title: ProbeBench design journal and client priming plan
content:
Purpose and scope:
This working journal captures a new benchmarking harness design ("ProbeBench") and an operational plan for deterministic client priming and warmup that improves throughput repeatability across heterogeneous GPU fleets. Goal is a lightweight, reproducible harness we can run nightly and during release candidate validation to catch throughput regressions and surface thermal/cold-cache failure modes.

High-level design principles (notes to self):
- Make the harness deterministic by controlling RNG seeds, request ordering, and tokenization anchors where possible.
- Separate client-side priming from server priming: clients should simulate realistic session affinity and pacing; the server priming stage should be recorded and repeatable (same prefix sets and kv-cache warm calls).
- Avoid overfitting to a single model shape; support a model profile descriptor (seq_len distribution, kv cache use, kv cache hit rate) that the harness can parameterize.
- Ensure thermal-aware scheduling: long runs should include periodic cool-down checks and record GPU temperature time series.
- Minimal ops footprint: harness should push metrics to our existing observability pipeline (prom/OTel) and emit artifacts for later offline analysis (trace tarball, client logs, seed manifest).

Core components:
- orchestrator (k8s job runner) that sequences priming -> ramp -> plateau -> decay windows with instrumented checkpoints.
- client emulator: supports sessioned clients, stateless spike generators, and steady streaming clients. Has options: --seed, --session-affinity=<percent>, --pacing-ms, --prefix-set-file, --tokenizer=hf/llama/ggml.
- priming manifest: JSON list of prefixes with deterministic mapping to request ids and seed values.
- results collector: collects per-request latency, token-level tail latencies, GPU occupancy, GPU temperature, memory alloc patterns, and kernel-level counters when available.

Repeatability checklist (runbook):
1) Build harness image with pinned dependencies (torch/onnxruntime/tensorrt shim hashes recorded).
2) Provision test pool with explicit GPU model list and driver/kernel versions.
3) Load model artifact pinned to build id + quantization spec.
4) Push priming manifest to object store and reference manifest sha256 in run metadata.
5) Choose RNG seed and store it in run metadata.
6) Start synchronous priming stage: 3 passes over manifest at client concurrency = 1 to populate KV caches predictably.
7) Wait stabilization window (default 30s) to let background GC and allocator settle.
8) Run ramp phase with linear concurrency increase to target over N minutes.
9) Hold plateau for M minutes collecting steady-state slices.
10) Run decay + cooldown to capture hysteresis effects.

Warmup / priming strategies compared (notes):
- Prefix sweep: iterate a small curated prefix set of 50 short prompts that exercise attention context edges. Advantage: consistent kv cache footprints. Disadvantage: may not reflect long-tail token shapes.
- Tokenized anchor sequences: use long tokens that force maximum KV usage then follow with short queries to measure marginal cost. Good for worst-case occupancy.
- Randomized prefix sampling with fixed seed: more diverse but slightly increased variance. Use when we want distributional fidelity.

Recommended default for nightly runs:
- Priming manifest: 30 curated prefixes (mix short/long), 1 deterministic seed.
- Stabilization: 45s.
- Ramp: 3 minutes to target concurrency.
- Plateau: 10 minutes with sliding 60s window reporting.
- Repeat runs: 3 repeats per configuration, with full artifact capture.

Client configs (example):
- steady client: --concurrency=64 --pacing-ms=0 --session-affinity=80 --prefix-set=priming_v1.json --seed=1997
- spike test: --burst-size=1024 --burst-interval-ms=60000 --pacing-ms=0 --seed=1997
- priming runner: --concurrency=1 --repeat=3 --prefix-set=priming_v1.json --seed=1997

Metrics of interest (and why):
- p50/p95/p99 latency per-token and end-to-end (to detect tail behavior).
- throughput (tokens/s and requests/s) over sliding windows (to detect oscillation).
- GPU occupancy % (time with active kernels) and SM utilization.
- GPU temperature and fan speed (thermal throttling correlate).
- Memory alloc/free churn (spike sources for fragmentation-induced latency).
- Kernel-level counters (when available) for attention/copy kernels.
- Request-level metadata: prefix-id, seed, session-id, model-variant.

Analysis approach:
- Compare paired runs using the same random seed and manifest sha. Use paired t-test or non-parametric bootstrap on p95 latencies across windows.
- Compute occupancy fingerprint: histogram of seq_len * batch_size for tokens generated during plateau. Use as a canonical workload descriptor.
- Thermal drift detection: correlate throughput drops with GPU temp crossing empirically determined threshold.

Operational pitfalls and mitigations (field notes):
- Problem: allocator fragmentation during long runs => slow tail increases.
  Mitigation: force periodic memory trim steps between lanes, measure with allocator hooks.
- Problem: background housekeeping (e.g., model swizzling) creates periodic latency spikes.
  Mitigation: run a discovery sweep in maintenance window and instrument library-level GC.
- Problem: client process jitter (GC in python clients) contaminating variance.
  Mitigation: use Go client for steady runs or run many light-weight worker processes with single-run life.

Unresolved questions / experiments to run:
- How many priming passes are needed to achieve 95% stable occupancy across GPU types? Initial hypothesis: 3 passes for small models, 6 for large models with multi-stage kernels.
- Can we design a micro-priming sequence that fills hot caches without producing real tokens (cheap)? Explore a lightweight nvtx-instrumented shim that calls internal kernel warm paths.
- Effect of quantization profiles on ramp-to-plateau variance: schedule experiments for q8a/q4f variants.

Quick links to current scripts and dashboards:
- harness runner: github.com/redwood-inference/bench-harness/tree/main/probebench
- nightly job: k8s/job/probebench-nightly in clusters/devops (PR link above)
- dashboard: graphs/d/throughput/probebench-nightly (Confluence link in linked artifacts)

Immediate next steps (TODOs):
- [ ] Lock down priming_v1.json (Priya) with 30 prefixes and provide tokenization anchors.
- [ ] Add GPU temperature export from node exporter to bench pipeline (Omar).
- [ ] Implement seed manifest hash check in orchestrator and fail if mismatch (Luca).
- [ ] Run 10 repeated runs across 3 GPU SKUs and capture artifacts (Maya).

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep priming manifests short and curated; long lists increase run time and ops costs.
- Document exact docker base + driver used in run metadata; tiny libc/driver diffs change kernel selection and invalidate comparisons.
- Consider a light-weight "probe-only" mode that exercises kernels without generating large artifact bundles for faster iteration.

Appendix A: sample priming manifest fragment (priming_v1.json)
[
  {"id":"pfx-001","prompt":"Translate: 'Hello world' -> Spanish","seed":1997},
  {"id":"pfx-002","prompt":"Summarize: short 8-token bio","seed":1997},
  {"id":"pfx-003","prompt":"Extend: long code docstring to 256 tokens","seed":1997}
]

Appendix B: shorthand run command (k8s job)
kubectl apply -f probebench-job.yaml --dry-run=client  # inspect
kubectl logs -f job/probebench-nightly -c harness

End of journal entry.

-- maya
